title: No remission without Christ’s satisfaction as surety under justice and wisdom
source_text: IV. Non decrevit autem Deus electis suis peccata remittere, nisi modo qui deceret ejus justitiam & sapientiam. Ideoque noluit ut immunes fierent a poenis quas peccata ab ipsis admissa merentur, nisi aliqua ratione satisfaceret justitiae ipsius peccatorum vindici, & sic manifestaretur quanto odio prosequitur peccatum. Ac proinde statuit nulli peccata condonare, aliter quam interveniente morte & passione Christi filii sui, quem dedit hominibus vadem, qui in se eorum peccata susciperet, & poenas eis debitas exantlaret: gravissimos cruciatus, tum anima, tum corpore perferendo, & tandem mortem crucis maledictam & ignominiosam pro eis ultro subeundo. Nec enim ulli peccata remittuntur, aut remissa sunt unquam, nisi merito atque intuitu satisfactionis Christi, olim aliquando praestandae, & nunc suo tempore praestitae.
pass_a_gloss: But God did not decree to remit sins to his elect except in a manner that would befit his justice and wisdom. And therefore he was unwilling that they should become immune from the penalties their admitted sins deserve unless in some way satisfaction were made to his justice, the avenger of sins, and thus it should be manifested with how great hatred he pursues sin. And accordingly he determined to pardon sins to no one otherwise than with the intervening death and passion of Christ his Son, whom he gave to men as a surety, who would take their sins upon himself and endure the penalties owed them—bearing most grievous torments in soul and body, and at last voluntarily undergoing for them the cursed and ignominious death of the cross. For sins are remitted to no one, nor have they ever been remitted, except by the merit and in view of Christ’s satisfaction, formerly someday to be rendered, and now in its time rendered.
pass_b_english: Justice and wisdom required a fitting mode: no immunity without satisfaction to avenging justice.
Only through Christ the surety’s death and passion—never without that merit in view.

choices.why: Christ as legal substitute bearing owed penalties.
